## When splitting whole clusters leaves too few to confirm on

The `cluster` argument of `discover_confirm()` assigns whole clusters to
one half of the split or the other. That keeps the two halves independent
at the cluster level, but the confirmation is left with half the clusters,
and its reference degrees of freedom are that number minus one. With eight
cohorts, the confirmation would rest on four, three degrees of freedom. The
package warns below twenty clusters in the confirmation half, which means
about forty in total.

The within-cluster design is the alternative for data nested in a small
number of clusters:

1. **Split within clusters.** Every cluster is cut in half at random
   (`strata = cluster`), so every cluster contributes participants to both
   halves and the confirmation keeps them all.
2. **Discover on the centered outcome.** Before the tree is grown, the
   outcome is centered on its cluster mean within each imputed dataset
   (`center_by = cluster`), so that cluster-level variables cannot stand
   in for differences between clusters.
3. **Confirm three ways.** The standard cluster-robust confirmation on the
   raw outcome; the same confirmation with cluster fixed effects; and a
   separate confirmation within each cluster.

`discover_confirm(cluster = , within = TRUE)` runs the sequence.

## Why the extra steps are needed

Because both halves contain the same clusters, a split that merely sorts
clusters with different outcome levels can replicate for the wrong reason.
Suppose cohorts differ in their average outcome, and some predictor tracks
cohort membership, a site characteristic, say. A tree grown on the raw
outcome will tend to split on that predictor, because it predicts the
outcome through the cohort differences; and the split will then pass a
cluster-robust confirmation, because the same cohorts, with the same
differences, sit in the confirmation half.

Centering the outcome at discovery removes the cluster differences before
the tree sees them. The fixed-effects confirmation removes them again at
confirmation, so each split's contrast is estimated from variation within
clusters only. The per-cluster confirmations show whether a split points
the same way in most clusters or rests on one.

## A worked example

Eight cohorts with their own intercepts, a real within-cohort effect of
`x1`, and a cohort proxy `x4` that tracks the cohort intercepts but has no
within-cohort relation to the outcome.

```{r data}
library(ctreeMI)
G <- 8; n_per <- 100; n <- G * n_per
cohort <- factor(rep(sprintf("c%02d", 1:G), each = n_per))
u  <- rnorm(G, 0, 0.6)[as.integer(cohort)]
x1 <- rnorm(n); x2 <- rnorm(n); x4 <- u + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)
y  <- u + 1.2 * (x1 > 0) + rnorm(n)
d  <- data.frame(y, x1, x2, x4, cohort)
d$x1[sample(n, 120)] <- NA
```

```{r run}
res <- discover_confirm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x4, data = d, m = 5,
                        cluster = "cohort", within = TRUE, seed = 7)
res$within
```

The tree split on `x1`, not on the proxy. The summary lines the three
confirmations up by split:

* `contrast` and `p_adj` are from the cluster-robust confirmation on the
  raw outcome. These are the estimates to report.
* `within` and `p_adj_within` are from the fixed-effects confirmation.
* `same_sign` counts the clusters whose own contrast shares the sign of the
  robust contrast, out of the clusters in which the split could be tested.
* `reading` is `confirmed within clusters` when both tests pass at alpha,
  `between-cluster difference` when the robust test passes but the
  fixed-effects test does not, and `not confirmed` otherwise.

The full confirmation objects are there for inspection:
`res$within$robust`, `res$within$within`, and `res$within$by_cluster`, a
list with one confirmation per cohort. `res$confirmation` is the robust
one, so `prune_unconfirmed()` and `report_confirm()` work as they do for
any other analysis.

```{r report}
report_confirm(res)
```

## What the claim is

With a whole-cluster split, a confirmed split is evidence about clusters the
tree never saw. With the within-cluster design, the claim is replication in
held-out participants from these clusters. How far that extends to other
clusters depends on how consistent the effect is across them, which is what
the per-cluster confirmations show: an effect that points the same way in
most clusters is unlikely to be an artifact of one or two.

## What the design has been checked against

The design was examined in a simulation with 5 to 20 cohorts, equal and
unequal cohort sizes, and null, moderate and weak within-cohort effects,
against the same split with the tree grown on the raw outcome and against
splitting whole cohorts. In short: growing the tree on the centered outcome
kept a cohort-level proxy out of the tree, nothing was confirmed within
clusters under the null, the fixed-effects test cost almost no power, and
unequal cohort sizes changed none of this. The script and results are
archived with the package's other simulations; the README gives the links.
Effects that differ in size between cohorts were not examined.

## Doing it by hand

The pieces are separate functions, for when the imputation model needs
control.

```{r hand, eval = FALSE}
parts <- split_holdout(d, strata = "cohort", seed = 42)
imp_d <- mice::mice(parts$discover, m = 30, seed = 1)   # cohort stays in
imp_c <- mice::mice(parts$confirm,  m = 30, seed = 2)   # the imputation model
tree  <- ctree_stacked(y ~ x1 + x2 + x4, data = imp_d, center_by = "cohort")
cw    <- confirm_within(tree, imp_c, cluster = "cohort")
```

`center_outcome()` is the centering step on its own; it scores an ordinal
outcome and expands a nominal one into centered indicators, and
`ctree_stacked()` grows a multivariate tree on the expansion while keeping
the original formula for the confirmation.
